questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: After the Western Roman Empire fell, why did large-scale trade and communication across Europe decline so sharply?
options: There was no central authority to maintain roads, protect trade routes, or enforce common laws
Everyone forgot how to read and write overnight
The Catholic Church banned all travel between regions
A new unified European currency failed and destroyed trade
questions.answer: There was no central authority to maintain roads, protect trade routes, or enforce common laws
questions.why: Rome's collapse removed the centralized administration, army, and infrastructure that had kept trade routes safe and functioning. Without that unifying power, regions became isolated and localized — this is the real cause of decline, not literacy or currency myths.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: In the feudal pyramid, what best describes the position of peasants (serfs)?
options: They worked the land and owed labour/goods to a lord, but had very limited freedom to leave
They owned their land outright and paid no obligations to anyone
They were paid wages by the king directly for farming
They ranked above knights but below vassals
questions.answer: They worked the land and owed labour/goods to a lord, but had very limited freedom to leave
questions.why: Serfs were bound to the land they worked and owed labour, crops, or goods to their lord in exchange for protection — they did not own land freely. A common misconception is confusing feudal obligation with paid employment or land ownership.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: In which century did William Shakespeare write and perform his plays?
options: The 16th/17th century (late 1500s-early 1600s)
The 14th century (1300s)
The 19th century (1800s)
The 18th century (1700s)
questions.why: Shakespeare lived 1564-1616, writing during the Elizabethan and Jacobean eras. Students often confuse his era with the medieval period (14th century) because Romeo and Juliet is set in an earlier-feeling Verona.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: What is 'dramatic irony' as used in Romeo and Juliet, for example in the final scene?
options: When the audience knows something a character on stage doesn't, creating tension
When a character says the exact opposite of what they mean as a joke
When the plot suddenly changes direction unexpectedly
When two characters have the same name by coincidence
questions.answer: When the audience knows something a character on stage doesn't, creating tension
questions.why: Dramatic irony is when the audience has information a character lacks — like knowing Juliet is alive when Romeo believes she's dead. Confusing it with plot twists or verbal sarcasm misses that it's specifically about the audience/character knowledge gap.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: How does Shakespeare use the oxymoron 'loving hate' (and similar phrases) in Romeo and Juliet to explore the play's themes?
options: It shows how love and violence/hate are tangled together throughout the play, especially through the feud
It proves that Romeo secretly hates Juliet the whole time
It's just wordplay with no thematic purpose
It shows that hate always defeats love in the end
questions.answer: It shows how love and violence/hate are tangled together throughout the play, especially through the feud
questions.why: Oxymorons like 'loving hate' capture how the Montague-Capulet feud (hate) and Romeo/Juliet's romance (love) are inseparable — the family hatred directly causes the tragedy of their love. It's not empty wordplay or a simple 'hate wins' message.

questions.subject: Science
questions.prompt: In an experiment testing how fertiliser amount affects plant height, what is the controlled variable?
options: Factors like water, sunlight, and soil type, which are kept the same for all plants
The amount of fertiliser given to each plant
The height of the plants measured at the end
The type of plant being grown, which is changed each trial
questions.answer: Factors like water, sunlight, and soil type, which are kept the same for all plants
questions.why: Controlled variables are the things kept constant so only the independent variable (fertiliser) affects the dependent variable (height). Mixing this up with the independent or dependent variable is the most common error.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: Why did the Crusades ultimately fail to achieve permanent Christian control of the Holy Land?
options: Christian forces could not hold territory long-term against determined Muslim resistance and reconquest, especially under leaders like Saladin
The Pope cancelled all future Crusades after the first one succeeded
European kings refused to send any soldiers after 1099
The Crusaders converted peacefully to Islam and stopped fighting
questions.answer: Christian forces could not hold territory long-term against determined Muslim resistance and reconquest, especially under leaders like Saladin
questions.why: Despite early successes like capturing Jerusalem in 1099, Crusader states were gradually reconquered, notably after Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187. The Crusades were a series of campaigns over centuries, not a single successful event, and the outcome was ultimately Muslim control being restored.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why the Catholic Church grew so powerful in medieval Europe after Rome's fall?
options: It was one of the few stable, organised institutions left, providing structure, education, and unifying authority across fragmented kingdoms
It had its own army that conquered all of Europe by force
Kings were legally required to hand over their thrones to the Pope
It was the only source of food and farming knowledge in Europe
questions.answer: It was one of the few stable, organised institutions left, providing structure, education, and unifying authority across fragmented kingdoms
questions.why: With Roman political structures gone, the Church stepped in as a unifying, literate, organised institution across fractured kingdoms — through monasteries, education, and moral authority, not military conquest.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: Romeo and Juliet is often described as a 'tragedy' — what does this genre label tell us about the play?
options: The story ends in death/downfall, often caused by a flaw or circumstance beyond the characters' full control
The story is meant to be entirely comedic and lighthearted
It means the play was based on a true historical event
It means the play has a happy ending after early struggles
questions.answer: The story ends in death/downfall, often caused by a flaw or circumstance beyond the characters' full control
questions.why: A tragedy in Shakespeare's sense ends in death or ruin, often driven by fate, flaw, or circumstance — Romeo and Juliet fits this through the feud and fateful timing. It is not a comedy, nor necessarily historical fact.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: What technique is Shakespeare using when Romeo compares Juliet to the sun ('But soft, what light through yonder window breaks? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun')?
options: Metaphor — directly describing Juliet as being the sun, not just similar to it
Simile — comparing Juliet to the sun using 'like' or 'as'
Personification — giving the sun human qualities
Alliteration — repeating the same starting sound
questions.answer: Metaphor — directly describing Juliet as being the sun, not just similar to it
questions.why: This is a metaphor because Romeo states Juliet IS the sun, without using 'like' or 'as' — that direct equation is what separates metaphor from simile. Students often mislabel this as simile due to the comparative feel.
